concepts.title: Heartache and Hemlock: Entering the Nightingale's World
concepts.definition: Keats opens with a heartache and drowsy numbness, as though of hemlock drunk or some opiate drained -- not envy of the nightingale's happiness but a shared too-much-happiness in its song. The bird sings of summer in full-throated ease among beeches and shadowy forest, and the poet longs to follow.
concepts.key_idea: Pain and happiness fused -- the nightingale's song produces a numbness that is half sorrow, half intoxication.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww121.txt opening stanzas (heart aches, drowsy numbness, hemlock, opiate, dryad sung beeches, summer in full throated ease)
question_patterns: how does keats describe his state at the start of the ode

solution_steps.explain: The heart aches into numbness, figured as hemlock or opiate -- song experienced as intoxication.
Keats denies envy: the ache is happiness too great for his dying-frame world to hold.
The nightingale, a dryad of the trees, sings of unpicked summer among beech greens.

concepts.title: Wine, the Nightingale and the Fade Far Away Wish
concepts.definition: The poet longs for a draught of vintage -- cool aching wine tasted of Flora and country green -- to leave the world unseen and fade away with the nightingale into the dim forest. He names the world where men sit and hear each other groan, where palsy shakes a few sad last grey hairs, where youth grows pale and dies -- the human realm of weariness, fever and fret.
concepts.key_idea: To fade with the bird -- escape imagined first as wine, then named as flight from a world of groans and grey hairs.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww121.txt middle stanzas (draught of vintage, flora and country green, fade far away, dissolve and quite forget, men sit and hear each other groan, palsy, youth grows pale, weariness fever and fret)

solution_steps.explain: A beaker of southern vintage -- tasting of Flora, dance and song -- seems the easy escape route.
He would fade with the nightingale into the forest dim, forgetting what the nightingale has never known.
Groaning men, shaking palsy, pale dying youth, leaden-eyed despairs -- the fever and fret of mortal life.

concepts.title: The Word Forlorn and the Return to the Sole Self
concepts.definition: At the climax the poet bids the bird farewells, wondering if this waking dream is vision or waking dream, unable to say whether he wakes or sleeps. The word 'forlorn' tolls him back to his sole self; the nightingale's song fades past the next valley, and the poem ends in the question -- do I wake or sleep?
concepts.key_idea: The bell that rings him home -- fancy cannot cheat so well, and the ode ends suspended between waking and sleep.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww121.txt closing stanzas (forlorn tolls back to the sole self, fancy cannot cheat so well, adieu, embalmed darkness, fading music past meadows and valley, do i wake or sleep)
question_patterns: why does the word forlorn toll the poet back to his sole self

solution_steps.explain: 'Forlorn' rings like a bell, dragging the imagination back from the bird's world to the solitary human one.
The music passes over meadows, up stream and hill, until it is plaintive only -- then gone.
Left asking whether he wakes or sleeps, the poet concedes fancy's cheat -- the immortal song outlasts the mortal listener.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Catalogue the human sufferings Keats lists as the world he wants to forget. What do they have in common?

solution_template.explain: Men groaning over their last grey hairs, youth growing pale and spectre-thin, beauty unable to keep her lustrous eyes.
Each is a face of ageing, illness and despair -- mortality wearing different masks.
Against the nightingale's effortless song, the stanza sets mortality's whole wardrobe -- hence the longing to fade away.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Explain the phrase 'fancy cannot cheat so well as she is famed to do'.

solution_template.explain: Fancy is the imagining power that built the whole forest escape.
The word 'forlorn' proves imagination's escape incomplete -- the self returns despite it.
Keats admits art's limits: it cheats wonderfully, but mortality reclaims the cheat.
